summary: שָׁמַיִם is the heavens: the sky above the earth where the birds fly, the stars are set and the rain and dew come from, and, with אֶרֶץ, the whole of what God made. It is also where Yahweh dwells, sits enthroned and hears, so that “the heavens” can stand for God himself (“the heavens rule”, Dan 4:23). The prophets use the heavens and the earth as a figure for a nation’s order of rulers and people, shaken in judgment or made new. Biblical Aramaic שְׁמַיִן and the Peshitta’s שְׁמַיָּא are the same word, with their own root spelling.

words.summary: Always plural in form. Its range runs from the air just above the ground to the dwelling of God; the context, and often a phrase (“birds of the heavens”, “God of the heavens”), shows which.

senses.definition: The expanse above the earth, which God named “heavens”: where the birds fly, the sun, moon and stars are set, the clouds gather, and rain, dew, hail and fire come down from. Its height is the measure of what is very high.

evidence.note: God called the expanse (רָקִיעַ) שָׁמָיִם.
Birds fly across the face of the expanse of the heavens.
The lights are set in the expanse of the heavens to shine on the earth.
Abram is told to look at the heavens and count the stars.
The windows of the heavens are closed and the rain from the heavens is held back.
Yahweh shuts up the heavens and there is no rain.
The dew of the heavens beside the fatness of the earth.
Moses stretches his staff toward the heavens and hail comes.
The heavens grow dark with clouds and wind before the rain.
The way of an eagle in the heavens.
A tower with its top in the heavens: the sky as the measure of height.
Cities great and fortified up to the heavens.
As the heavens are higher than the earth, so Yahweh’s ways are higher than man’s.
Elijah goes up in a whirlwind into the heavens, carried up into the sky.
The Peshitta’s שְׁמַיָּא for the red sky of the weather sign.

senses.definition: With אֶרֶץ, the heavens and the earth together name all that God made, above and below.

evidence.note: God created the heavens and the earth.

God Most High, possessor of heavens and earth.
Yahweh, maker of heavens and earth.
You made the heavens, the heavens of the heavens and all their host, the earth and all on it.
Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?
The New Testament prayer to the God who made the heaven and the earth and the sea.

senses.definition: The heavens and the earth are called on to hear and to bear witness when Yahweh sets his covenant before his people.

evidence.note: I call the heavens and the earth to witness against you today.
Give ear, heavens, and let the earth hear.
Hear, heavens, and give ear, earth, for Yahweh has spoken.

senses.definition: The heavens as the place where Yahweh dwells and sits enthroned, from which he looks down, hears prayer, speaks and acts on the earth. They do not contain him.

evidence.note: Hear in the place of your dwelling, in the heavens, and forgive.
Yahweh, his throne is in the heavens.
The heavens are my throne and the earth my footstool.
God is in the heavens and you are on the earth.
He who sits in the heavens laughs.
Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.
Look down from your holy dwelling, from the heavens.

I have spoken with you from the heavens.
The angel of Yahweh calls to Abraham from the heavens.
The heavens and the heavens of the heavens cannot contain you.
Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God in the heavens.
Heaven is the throne of God (Peshitta שְׁמַיָּא, Isa 66:1).

senses.gloss: heavens and earth as a figure for a nation’s order
senses.definition: In the prophets the heavens (with the earth, the sun, moon and stars) stand for a nation’s ruling order: shaken, darkened or rolled up when Yahweh overthrows a kingdom, and planted or created new when he establishes his people.

evidence.note: “I am shaking the heavens and the earth”, explained in the next verse as the overthrow of the throne of kingdoms (Hag 2:22).
The heavens rolled up like a scroll and their host withering, because Yahweh’s sword comes down on Edom (Isa 34:5-6).
The heavens tremble and the earth shakes in the burden of Babylon (Isa 13:1), whose stars and sun go dark (13:10) when Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, is overthrown (13:19).
To plant the heavens and found the earth is to say to Zion, “You are my people.”
New heavens and a new earth: Jerusalem created a rejoicing and her people a joy (Isa 65:18).
The heavens and earth Isaiah calls to hear are addressed again in 1:10 as the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah.
Judah’s land without form and the heavens without light, in Jeremiah’s vision of its overthrow.
The new heavens and new earth stand before Yahweh as Israel’s seed and name will stand.
New heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells, Isaiah’s promise awaited.

Heavens for height and earth for depth.

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel, Ezra and Jer 10:11, always in the emphatic שְׁמַיָּא. Beside the sky and the dwelling of God it once stands for God himself: “the heavens rule”.

senses.definition: The sky above the earth: its birds, its dew, its winds and clouds, and the height a great tree reaches.

evidence.note: עוֹף שְׁמַיָּא, the birds of the heavens.
Wet with the dew of the heavens.
The four winds of the heavens stir up the great sea.
The tree’s height reaches to the heavens.
With the clouds of the heavens one like a son of man came.

senses.definition: With אֲרַע, all that God made; the idols made neither.

evidence.note: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish from under these heavens.
Servants of the God of heavens and earth.
Signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth.

senses.definition: Where God is, from which he reveals, rules and sends his messengers; he is “the God of the heavens”, “the King of the heavens”, “the Lord of the heavens”.

evidence.note: There is a God in the heavens who reveals secrets.
The God of the heavens will set up a kingdom.
A watcher, a holy one, coming down from the heavens.
The King of the heavens.
The Lord of the heavens.
The house of the God of the heavens.

senses.definition: “The heavens” used for the God who rules from them.

evidence.note: “The heavens rule” (דִּי שַׁלִּטִן שְׁמַיָּא), restating the verse before, “the Most High rules in the kingdom of man” (Dan 4:22).
ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, Dan 7:13’s “clouds of the heavens”.
The kingdoms under all the heavens given to the saints.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s word for heaven, about 300 times in its New Testament, with the Hebrew’s range: the sky, the dwelling of God, heaven standing for God, and heaven and earth together.

senses.definition: The sky with its birds, stars, clouds and weather.

evidence.note: The birds of the sky.
The face of the sky, red and overcast.
The stars will fall from the sky.

senses.definition: Where the Father is and his throne, from which the son came down and to which he went up.

evidence.note: Our Father in the heavens.
Heaven is the throne of God.
Isa 66:1 quoted.
No one has gone up to heaven but the one who came down from heaven.
Jesus taken up into heaven, to come in the same way.
Christ entered heaven itself, to appear before God for us.

senses.definition: Heaven named in place of God, as the source of authority or the one sinned against.

evidence.note: “I have sinned against heaven and before you.”
John’s baptism, “from heaven or from men?”
מַלכֻּותָֿא דַּשמַיָא, the kingdom of heaven, which Mark calls the kingdom of God (Mrk 1:15).

senses.definition: With אַרְעָא, the present order and the new heaven and earth promised in Isaiah.

evidence.note: New heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.
The present heavens and earth kept for fire.

words.summary: Formed from שְׁמַיָּא as אַרְעָנָיָא is from אַרְעָא, and set against it.

senses.definition: Of or from heaven, as against what is of the earth.

evidence.note: Heavenly bodies beside earthly bodies (אַרעָנָיֵא).

cognates.gloss: sky, heaven, the canopy of the earth; the upper part of anything; roof; clouds; rain

cognates.note: Arabic s answers to Hebrew shin (š), not to ṯ, which Arabic writes ث. Lane files the noun under the verb سَمَا "was high, lofty" (p. 1433, n20811), and, like the Akkadian, it also names the rain that comes from the sky.

cognates.gloss: of the sky or heaven, heavenly, celestial

evidence.locator: p. 1435, root سمو, سَمَآئِىٌّ and سَمَاوِىٌّ (n20829)
evidence.note: "[Of, or relating to, the sky or heaven; heavenly; celestial;] rel. ns. from سَمَآءٌ".

cognates.note: The adjective formed from the sky-word, as Syriac שְׁמַיָּנָא is from שְׁמַיָּא.

evidence.note: "/šamūma/, gen.-acc. /šamīma/, cf. ša-mu-ma U:V:137:III:13′, “heaven” (cf. H. šāmáyim, Aram. det. šəmayyā; cf. Arab. samāʾ, Akkad. šamū pl.)".
ʿṣr.šmm, "birds of the heavens", parallel to "fish(es) from/of the sea" (1.23:63), as עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם beside דְּגַת הַיָּם (Gen 1:26).
šmm.šmn.tmṭrn, "heavens will rain oil": the heavens as the source of rain.
Ugaritic šmm "heavens" beside common Ethiopic samāy, pl. samāyāt, "sky, heaven(s)".

cognates.note: Ugaritic keeps š and ṯ apart, and writes š here. Like the Hebrew, the word is plural in form, and it has the Hebrew’s phrases “birds of the heavens” and heavens that rain.

evidence.note: Meanings "heaven; heaven, sky; rain; sky".
Meanings "heaven; heavens; sky".

cognates.note: Akkadian š stands for both older š and ṯ, so it does not show the sound. Segert gives the Akkadian as plural (šamū), as the Hebrew is.

cognates.gloss: heavens; the great heavens, the residence of the gods

evidence.note: "[Heb. šamayim] n.pl. HEAVENS": KAI 147.3 (Neo-Punic) hšmm, "facing heaven they prayed"; Plautus, Poenulus 1027, Bal samem, "Baal [of] the heavens".
"THE GREAT HEAVENS, in Ph religion of the second half of the first millennium B.C. the residence of the gods", KAI 14.16-17.

cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic, plural as in Hebrew. “Baal of the heavens” is the Canaanite counterpart of “the God of the heavens”; the Phoenicians set their gods to dwell in “the great heavens”, as scripture sets Yahweh’s dwelling in the heavens and denies that they contain him (1Ki 8:27).

evidence.note: "ns smyn C540/82+ HEAVEN (only in divine epithets) [Eth samāy, Ar samāʾ id.]": ʾlhn bʿl smyn wʾrḍn "(the) God, Lord of heaven and earth"; RḤMNN dbsmyn "(the god) R. who is in heaven" (C542/7).

cognates.note: Sabaic, whose s¹ answers to Hebrew shin. “Lord of heaven and earth” is the pairing of Gen 14:19, and “who is in heaven” that of Ecc 5:1. The y kept here is the third root letter Fisher notes the Ethiopic also keeps.

evidence.note: "Com. Eth ሰማይ samāy (pl. ሰማያት samāyāt) ‘sky, heaven(s)’ preserves the third radical, y, of the ESA smyn".

cognates.note: Ge’ez s answers to Hebrew shin. Cited from Fisher’s comparison; the Ge’ez dictionaries themselves (Dillmann, Leslau) are not yet checked.

evidence.note: "= h. שָׁמַיִם, heaven; trnsf. God": Targ. Gen. 1:1; Targ. Deut. 10:14.

cognates.note: The Aramaic of the Targums and Talmud, where, as in Dan 4:23, heaven stands for God. Aramaic writes older ṯ as ת, so its ש shows š.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh made the heavens and the earth, the sea and all that is in them, in six days, and rested on the seventh (Exo 20:11; 31:17). On the second day he named the expanse “heavens” (Gen 1:8), and on the fourth he set the lights in the expanse of the heavens (Gen 1:17-19). The heavens were made by his word and the breath of his mouth (Psa 33:6), and he stretched them out by himself (Isa 44:24). That he made the heavens is what sets him apart from the gods of the nations, which are idols (Psa 96:5; Jer 10:11).

Psalm 115:16 divides the two realms: the heavens are Yahweh’s, and the earth he has given to the sons of man. The heavens are where Yahweh sits enthroned and hears (Psa 11:4; 1Ki 8:30; Isa 66:1), and the Preacher makes the contrast a rule for prayer: God is in the heavens and you are on the earth (Ecc 5:1). The earth is man’s place, and the promises to the faithful are promises of the earth: the meek will inherit it (Mat 5:5), and the redeemed will reign on it (Rev 5:10).

No one has gone up to heaven except the son of man who came down from it (Jhn 3:13). Peter says the same of David: he died and was buried, his tomb is still with us, and he did not go up to the heavens (Act 2:29, 34). Job says the dead lie down and do not rise “until the heavens are no more”; they do not wake from their sleep (Job 14:12). Elijah went up “in a whirlwind into the heavens” (2Ki 2:11), into the sky, not to the dwelling of God: a writing from him later reached Jehoram king of Judah (2Ch 21:12), who began to reign (2Ki 8:16) after Elisha had already taken Elijah’s place (2Ki 3:11). Heaven is God’s dwelling, not where the dead go; the one man there is Jesus, whom heaven must receive until he returns in the same way he went (Act 1:11; 3:21).

Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar that the God of the heavens will set up a kingdom that will crush the kingdoms of men and stand for ever (Dan 2:44); it is given to the saints as the kingdoms “under all the heavens” (Dan 7:27), a kingdom on the earth. In Daniel 4 “the heavens rule” (Dan 4:23, 4:26 in English Bibles) restates the verse before, “the Most High rules in the kingdom of man” (Dan 4:22): heaven stands for God. So Matthew’s “kingdom of the heavens” (Mat 3:2; 4:17) is the kingdom of God, as Mark words the same preaching (Mrk 1:15): the kingdom whose ruler is in heaven and whose source is heaven, not a kingdom in the sky. Jesus taught his disciples to pray that it come and that God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven (Mat 6:10), and when it comes the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of God and his anointed (Rev 11:15).

The prophets use the heavens and the earth for a nation’s order of rulers and people. Isaiah calls the heavens and the earth to hear (Isa 1:2), and addresses them again as the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah (Isa 1:10). In the burden of Babylon the stars and sun go dark and the heavens tremble (Isa 13:1, 10, 13) when Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, is overthrown (Isa 13:19). The heavens rolled up like a scroll are explained by the sword that comes down on Edom (Isa 34:4-5), and Haggai’s shaking of the heavens and the earth is the overthrow of the throne of kingdoms (Hag 2:21-22). Yahweh “plants the heavens and founds the earth” when he says to Zion, “You are my people” (Isa 51:16). So the new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65:17 are a new order on the earth, in which Jerusalem is created a rejoicing and men live long, build houses and plant vineyards (Isa 65:18, 20-21). This is the promise Peter waits for: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2Pe 3:13).

note: Root: the database keys the Hebrew noun’s tokens under שמה, BDB’s heading for it, so the entry takes שמה (no existing entry has it). Scripture has no verb of this root; the noun is plural in form in Hebrew, Ugaritic, Phoenician and Akkadian. Lane files Arabic samāʾ under سمو “was high” and Fisher notes that Sabaic smyn and Ge’ez samāy keep a third root letter y; whether the noun comes from a root “be high” is a lead not followed, and is not asserted. The Aramaic word has its own key שמינ (BDB xv.au.ab), so a brief for שמה misses it. Left out: שָׁמָּה “there” (v.dy.ad, under שָׁם), and שְׁמוּאֵל and שְׁמִידָע, which BDB lists here only to refer them to שֵׁם. שַׁמְהוּת Shamhuth (v.dy.ae, 1Ch 27:8) is left without a name entry, as the task expected none; its derivation from this root is unclear (שׁמם “be desolate” is the other candidate). Daniel is cited in the Hebrew text’s numbering: Dan 4:22-23 here are 4:25-26 in English Bibles. Leads not followed: Leslau 1987 and Dillmann 1865 for Ge’ez samāy (cited only from Fisher); DULAT for Ugaritic šmm; Hoftijzer-Jongeling for Old Aramaic šmyn; CAD Š/1 for šamû.
